newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Bayer to continue evaluating Taiwan chemical plant.
newsitem.headline: Bayer to continue evaluating Taiwan chemical plant.

text.p: German chemicals group Bayer AG would continue its evaluation on a T$49 billion chemicals plant in Taiwan despite protests from local environmental groups, a Bayer executive said on Wednesday.

"The company's board meeting has decided to continue discussing the investment project with Taiwan authorities," Chen Chai-chung, Bayer's vice president in Taiwan, told reporters, broadcast on state television.
Bayer planned to build the plant in central Taichung. The plant will produce TDI, a mid-stream chemical material for producing synthetic leather.
Bayer would continue its evaulation here but the company did not rule out the possibility of moving the project to Thailand or the United States, Chen said.
A final decision would be made by the end of 1996, he added.

The multi-million project has received a great attention on the island and the government said it would do its best to help finalise the project, which would become one of the biggest foreign investments in Taiwan.
The cabinet agreed in August to lend Bayer 72 hectares of state land in Taichung at a low rent for 50 years. But local environmental groups have launched protest against the Bayer project.
Chen said the company is confident to pursuade local people to accept the project after making a final decision.
"Environmental protest can be found in every advanced democratic country," Chen said.
"Based on our environmental technology, experience and communication skill...we have the confidence to convince local people to accept."
The project will fall into three stages, with the first stage -- costing T$11.5 billion -- expected to start construction in September, a Taiwan official has said.
The first stage will be completed in late 1998, while completion for the third stage is slated for 2004.
The plant will focus on exports, especially the mainland China market.

Taiwan hopes to turn the island into a regional operation centre for multinational firms. The government has offered a series of preferential treatments such as tax credits to attract foreign investment to Taiwan.
